Alert: HighErrorRate on io-shop
What the alert said [AL1]: Error rate above threshold for 5m {A1}

Argus first posted about the incident in Slack at 2026-11-11T02:04:49Z {first_told}, and the document says so already: leave that post out, and do not say that no person was told. That nobody was paged is a finding of its own.
The alert rule waits 5 minutes {rule_waits} with its condition holding before it fires. The alert came 6 minutes 26 seconds {detection_gap} after its series passed its line, within the 7 minutes 30 seconds {accounted_for} accounted for by its rule waiting 5 minutes {rule_waits} with its condition holding, its evaluation at intervals of 1 minute {rule_evaluated_every}, an unmeasured allowance of 30 seconds {scraping_allowance} for scraping and storing its samples and the whole minute its series is read in.
Broken from 2026-11-11T01:57:00Z {began} (the onset) to 2026-11-11T02:06:00Z {back_to_normal}, when the metrics show it back to normal.
That is 9 minutes {duration}, and every impact figure below is measured over that stretch.
Argus held the incident for 2 minutes 20 seconds {held}, until 2026-11-11T02:07:07Z {argus_stopped}. That is not how long the fault lasted, nor how long Argus went on working - leave it out of your answer.
The service's error rate over all its requests, before it began: 1.0% {errors_before}.
The same rate while it was broken: 18.7% {errors_while_broken}, peaking at 26.0% {errors_at_worst}.
Rise above baseline: 17.7% {errors_rise} of traffic failed that otherwise would not have.
The series behind the alert, `sum(rate(http_requests_total{code=~"5.."}[1m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total[1m]))` - its alert said "Error rate above threshold for 5m {A1}" - which its alert rule evaluates and calls worse rising: 1.0166666666666666% {series_before} before it began, 18.722222222222223% {series_while_broken} on average while it was broken, and 26% {series_at_worst} at its worst. Say what it measures in words, not by its query.
Customer loss: 3,262.30 USD {customer_loss} - how far the shop's takings over the incident fell short of the same hours whole weeks earlier, beyond how much those hours vary on their own.

What Code-Fix read in the source, in Code-Fix's words - nothing ran to check it, and what it claims is not what happened unless a row of the record shows it:
  - [F1] Yes. The patch moves this revision's reader to a versioned key (`summary_key`), but nothing in this repository writes entries into the cache. `SummaryEntry.__str__` produces the text, and the lookup seam `LookUpSummary` is supplied from outside, so the code that stores entries lives elsewhere. Today that outside writer puts '2400/8 {F1.1}' under the bare shopper id, which is the key replicas still on 5470c1a6 read. Until it writes under `summary_key(shopper_id)` instead, those replicas keep meeting two-field entries and keep failing. The patch alone wouldn't spare users anything: worse, this revision would stop reading its own entries, which only makes it slower. To fix this, the cache-population code outside this repo has to write under `summary_key(shopper_id)` (`summary-v2:{shopper_id}`). Or it has to stop writing the two-field shape under the old key until no replica runs 5470c1a6. Separately, the old revision's reader is already deployed and can only be changed by shipping a new build, not from this repo's current code.

The document, by field:
root_cause: The new code changed what a summary cache entry holds, from a bare figure in cents to an 'amount/items' text, and wrote it where the previous version also reads, with no versioned key or other way to keep the two shapes apart. Replicas still on the previous version share that cache during the paused rolling update, and their reader expects a bare cents figure, so it raised ValueError on the new entries and the account page request failed.
cause_in_plain_words: A software update changed the format the shop uses to save each shopper's spending summary, and the copies of the shop still running the previous version expected the old format, could not read the new entries, and failed the account page.
still_at_risk: Deploying the same revision again, or any revision that writes the two-field cache entries, could make account pages fail again while replicas of the earlier revision are still serving.
symptom: Account pages failed for some shoppers
causal_chain 1: Shoppers' account page requests failed, and the share of the service's requests that failed rose well above its usual level. (cites AL1; G3714, under "Log lines it read, one per message"; Gbac1, under "Log lines it read, one per message")
causal_chain 2: Those requests failed because reading the shopper's summary cache entry in src/io_shop/summary_cache.py raised a ValueError: the entry was an 'amount/items' text, not a figure in cents. (cites G3714, under "Log lines it read, one per message"; Gc956, under "Log lines it read, one per message")
causal_chain 3: Entries in that two-field shape came from revision 696c33a, deployed at {P2.1}. It changed a cache entry from a bare figure in cents to one text holding the figure and the number of purchases behind it. (cites P2, under "Changes to production it read"; D1, under "What each deployment it looked into changed")
causal_chain 3 ruled_out 1: The earlier deploy of revision 5470c1a (P1). The metrics read back over the hours after it show the service at its usual error rate until the onset, account pages logged as rendering normally after it, and the confirmed rollback left that revision running with the service back to normal. (cites T5, under "What Argus did, in order"; Gad41, under "Log lines it read, one per message"; M1, under "Actions it took"; T23, under "What Argus did, in order")
causal_chain 4: The new shape broke pages because, as read at {T10.1}, the rolling update was paused with {T10.5} replicas still on revision 5470c1a, and those replicas could not read the two-field entries. (cites T10, under "What Argus did, in order"; D1, under "What each deployment it looked into changed"; Gc956, under "Log lines it read, one per message")
contributing_factors 1: No check was seen that tested the change against the previous revision reading the same cache, such as a mixed-version compatibility test, before a change to the shape of a shared cache entry went out.
contributing_factors 1 had_it_been_otherwise: The old reader's failure on the new entry shape would have been found before the deploy, and the change would not have reached production in a form the running replicas could not read.
contributing_factors 2: The previous revision's cache reader fails the account page when it meets an entry it cannot read, instead of treating the entry as a miss and working the figure out, which is what the module's own docstring says should happen.
contributing_factors 2 had_it_been_otherwise: Replicas on the old revision would have skipped the new entries and rendered the page more slowly, and the format mismatch would not have failed requests.
contributing_factors 3: No rollout health gate was seen that halts and rolls back an io-shop rolling update when errors rise. The rollout stayed in place, with both revisions serving, until Argus rolled it back.
contributing_factors 3 had_it_been_otherwise: The rolling update would have been reverted automatically once errors rose, ending the failures sooner.
action_items 1: Add a CI test that runs the previous revision's summary cache reader against entries written by the new revision, and the reverse, so a change to a shared entry shape cannot ship if a mixed rollout would break it.
action_items 2: Make it a review rule that any change to the shape of a shared cache entry either writes under a new versioned key or first ships a reader that accepts both shapes, before the writer changes.
action_items 3: Add a test that every summary cache reader treats an entry it cannot parse as a miss and falls back to working out the figure, never failing the page.
action_items 4: Add an error-rate health gate to io-shop rolling updates that halts the rollout and rolls it back automatically when the error rate rises above its baseline.
action_items 5: Route the HighErrorRate alert on io-shop to on-call paging so that a person is paged when it fires.
went_well 5: The Code-Fix Agent kept none of the fix it wrote, once its reading showed the fix would help only together with a change outside the repository.
went_wrong 1: Nobody was paged: the HighErrorRate alert on io-shop was not linked to any on-call incident.

Not to be judged:
  - Names in braces, such as {T5.1} or {duration}, are figures code writes in from the row they name. They are not judged.
  - Action items propose what to do; they make no claim about the record.
  - Whether something went well, went wrong or was lucky is a judgement. Only a fact it states is judged.

Judge every claim in the document, and answer by calling judge_claims.

tools.description: Submit every claim in the document, each either as supported or as flagged. Supported: the document's own words, quoted exactly, and the record's rows that support it. Flagged: the document's own words, quoted exactly, why, and the record's rows that contradict it (none where no row speaks to it at all). Empty lists say the document makes no claim to judge.

why.description: One sentence: what the record holds instead. Never empty.
